content: Hydralazine is available in oral tablet forms, including 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg doses, as well as in injectable forms. It should be stored at room temperature (68°F to 77°F or 20°C to 25°C) and kept in a cool, dry place, tightly closed. For short periods, it can tolerate temperatures between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). The most common side effects of hydralazine include headache, decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, a pounding or fast heartbeat, and chest pain or discomfort. If these side effects bother you, consult your healthcare provider. Serious side effects, though less common, include lupus-like symptoms (rash, joint pain, fever, weakness, swollen glands, or changes in urination), chest pain (potentially indicating a heart attack), blood disorders (such as agranulocytosis, anemia, or low white blood cell count), and nerve problems (peripheral neuropathy, including numbness, tingling, or paresthesia). If you experience any of these, contact your healthcare provider immediately. Hydralazine should not be used by individuals allergic to its ingredients, those with coronary artery disease (CAD), or those with mitral valve damage caused by rheumatic heart disease. In CAD, hydralazine can increase the workload on the heart, potentially leading to a heart attack. Similarly, in mitral valve disease, the increased blood flow to the heart can strain the valve and worsen the condition. Patients should use hydralazine only as prescribed by their healthcare provider. It should not be shared with others, even if they have similar conditions, as it may harm them. Hydralazine can affect alertness and coordination, so avoid driving or performing activities requiring focus until you know how the medication affects you. Before starting hydralazine, inform your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions and any medications, including prescription, over-the-counter, vitamins, or supplements, that you are taking. This is crucial to avoid potential drug interactions or complications.
